title: AI Agent Observability: Traces, Metrics, and Debugging
excerpt: Design AI agent observability around verified outcomes, useful traces, bounded metrics, safe redaction, and dashboards that lead to concrete action.
content:
AI agent observability should let an operator answer three questions: what outcome did the user receive, which execution decisions produced it, and what can be changed safely? Token charts alone answer none of them. A useful design connects task outcomes to workflow transitions, retrieval evidence, model requests, tool effects, and deployment versions.

This guide proposes an illustrative observability design for a support-resolution agent. Field names and thresholds are design examples, not a standardized agent telemetry schema or a tested implementation.

## Start with outcomes and execution identity

Define a small outcome vocabulary before instrumenting individual model calls. For the example service, a run finishes as resolved, escalated, cancelled, failed, or awaiting an external response. Record whether that classification is provisional or verified. An agent saying “resolved” is different from the customer system confirming the requested update.

Give every task a stable run identifier and every resumed execution a separate attempt identifier. A trace identifier belongs to telemetry; the business run identifier belongs to durable workflow state. Keeping both prevents a tracing-library restart or a sampling decision from erasing the application's ability to reconcile work.

Persist the final business outcome independently of trace export. Otherwise an observability outage can make the operational dashboard report fewer failures merely because failed executions stopped sending spans. Link the outcome record to trace identifiers when available, and count missing trace coverage as a separate instrumentation problem.

## Trace operations that explain decisions

OpenTelemetry represents operations as spans with timing, context, attributes, events, and relationships. Context propagation connects spans across services; span links can connect causally related asynchronous work. These primitives provide a foundation for agent telemetry without requiring a proprietary trace format. [OpenTelemetry traces](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/).

For the proposed support agent, use a root execution span and meaningful child operations:

| Operation | Useful diagnostic evidence | What it should not imply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retrieve policy | Index version, document identifiers, filter class, result count | Retrieved evidence is correct |
| Request model decision | Model identifier, prompt version, elapsed time, usage | A fluent answer is a successful task |
| Validate proposed action | Schema version, accepted flag, rejection category | Authorization has been granted |
| Execute tool | Tool name, operation identity, outcome class | A timeout means no effect occurred |
| Verify resolution | Required postcondition, evidence reference, verification result | The customer necessarily accepts the result |

Keep a logical tool operation separate from its network attempts. One refund proposal might produce three requests because of retries. Representing those as three unrelated successful actions makes both debugging and accounting misleading.

Capture transition events such as approval requested, approval expired, budget exhausted, and verification failed. Prefer machine-readable reason codes to prose that must be searched manually. Do not collect hidden model reasoning as an observability requirement; observable inputs, outputs, tool decisions, and verification evidence are the relevant operational contract.

Long waits deserve special handling. An approval that takes six hours should not appear as six hours of model inference. Record active processing, queue delay, and human waiting separately. A resumed worker can start another trace linked to the same durable run, preserving causality without keeping an execution span open indefinitely.

## Measure quantities with explicit denominators

Create metrics from authoritative lifecycle events rather than reconstructing all aggregates from sampled traces. The following names are illustrative application metrics:

- `agent_runs_total{workflow,outcome}` counts one terminal outcome per run.
- `agent_run_duration_seconds{workflow,outcome}` measures end-to-end time for a defined lifecycle.
- `agent_tool_attempts_total{tool,result_class}` exposes retry and dependency behavior.
- `agent_verification_total{check,result}` separates proposed completion from verified completion.
- `agent_queue_wait_seconds{workflow}` identifies admission and scheduling pressure.

Define the denominator of every ratio. “Resolution rate” could mean resolved runs divided by all submitted tasks, eligible tasks, or completed tasks. Those measures diverge when a backlog grows. Display submission volume, pending volume, and completion outcomes together so a stalled queue cannot look like improving quality.

Prometheus warns that every distinct label combination creates another time series and advises against unbounded labels such as user identifiers. Apply that constraint to agent identifiers too: run IDs, trace IDs, document URLs, and raw prompts do not belong in metric labels. [Prometheus metric and label guidance](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/).

Use bounded workflow names and outcome categories for aggregation. Put per-run correlation in traces or access-controlled event storage. Even bounded dimensions multiply: ten workflows, four outcomes, and five deployment rings already create 200 combinations before histogram buckets. Review the full combination space rather than approving each label independently.

For cost attribution, connect usage events to the same run identity while preserving provider-reported versus locally estimated values. The companion guide on [agent cost budgets](/blog/ai-agent-cost-budgets) develops that accounting boundary.

## Work through a misleading success signal

Consider a hypothetical incident: the model provider reports successful HTTP responses, but users receive unresolved tickets. An operator opens the task dashboard and sees a rising verification-failed outcome, concentrated in a recently deployed prompt version.

A representative trace shows policy retrieval returning zero authorized documents. The model still proposes an answer, the output passes schema validation, and a final policy-evidence check rejects it. The dependency worked, the model request worked, and the task failed. Grouping all three layers under one “error rate” would conceal the mechanism.

The next debugging step is to compare successful and failed runs with the same workflow and document-index version. If both prompt versions fail only for one document class, retrieval filtering is the stronger lead. If failures align with the new prompt across document classes, inspect how it handles missing evidence. These are investigation hypotheses, not causal conclusions from a chart.

Once the defect is understood, preserve a sanitized failing case in the regression dataset. Observability supplies a reproducible failure description; evaluation determines whether the proposed correction improves task behavior without introducing another regression.

## Sample traces without rewriting reality

OpenTelemetry distinguishes head sampling, decided early, from tail sampling, which uses information from much or all of a trace. Head sampling alone cannot ensure retention of every trace containing a later error. Tail sampling adds buffering and operational complexity. [OpenTelemetry sampling](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/sampling/).

For the example service, retain a representative baseline plus additional traces for verification failures, unusual loop counts, and selected rollout cohorts. Record the sampling policy so investigators know whether an apparent pattern is a collection artifact.

Do not estimate population success rates directly from an intentionally failure-heavy trace sample. Use lifecycle metrics for population totals and sampled traces for explanations. Also remember that a downstream tail sampler cannot recover spans already dropped upstream.

Track telemetry health itself: exporter failures, dropped spans, collector queue depth, and the proportion of terminal run records with usable trace references. A beautiful dashboard backed by an overloaded collector is an unreliable witness.

## Redact before data leaves the process

OpenTelemetry's sensitive-data guidance emphasizes minimizing collection and reviewing what instrumentation libraries emit. Collector processors can remove, transform, or filter attributes, but automatic instrumentation does not know your application's sensitivity boundaries. [Handling sensitive telemetry data](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/security/handling-sensitive-data/).

In this proposed design, allowlist metadata at instrumentation points. Record document IDs and versions instead of entire retrieved documents. Capture argument names and validation categories instead of access tokens or full request bodies. Exception messages need scrutiny because database clients and HTTP libraries may embed sensitive values in them.

Keep any approved content captures in a separate restricted store with explicit retention, access logging, and deletion handling. A trace can carry an opaque evidence reference. That reference must not become a publicly accessible URL or bypass tenant authorization.

Test redaction with synthetic secrets before deployment. Put recognizable canary values in prompts, tool errors, URLs, and headers, then inspect every exporter and backend. Checking only the application logger misses framework-generated spans and collector debug outputs.

## Build dashboards that lead to an action

Google's SRE workbook recommends moving from user-impacting SLO signals to diagnostic metrics and monitoring deployed binaries, configuration, and dependencies. For an agent, prompt, tool-schema, retrieval-index, and policy versions are additional useful change records. [Google SRE monitoring](https://sre.google/workbook/monitoring/).

A practical dashboard starts with task outcomes, pending work, latency, and verified action failures. Its second layer breaks these down by bounded workflow and release cohort. A third layer links to representative traces, recent changes, and the relevant recovery procedure.

Page an operator for conditions requiring timely intervention, not for every model refusal. A refusal may be a correct policy outcome. Give an alert an owner, a user-impact description, and a first containment action. Connect that action to the controls described in [agent incident response](/blog/ai-agent-incident-response).

Before relying on the dashboard, inject a tool timeout, a lost export batch, missing retrieval evidence, and a cancelled run. Confirm that business outcomes remain counted, traces explain the sequence when retained, and alerts distinguish workflow failure from telemetry failure.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is model-provider monitoring enough?

It covers the provider interaction, not your retrieval, authorization, external effects, or verified task outcome. Instrument those application boundaries independently.

### Should every token become a span?

Usually a model request is the useful operation boundary. Per-token spans can create substantial volume without clarifying the workflow. Record streaming milestones only when they answer a specific latency question.

### Must every run retain its full transcript?

No. Keep enough structured evidence to diagnose the service while honoring access and retention constraints. Selective, authorized content capture can support difficult cases without making unrestricted transcript storage the default.
researchNote: Read primary OpenTelemetry trace, sampling, and sensitive-data documentation; Prometheus label guidance; and the Google SRE monitoring chapter on 2026-11-10. The metric names, support-agent scenario, sampling policy, and dashboard design are illustrative engineering proposals, not tested implementation or benchmark claims. Avoided unstable GenAI semantic attribute names because the old specification page now points to a relocated repository.
